question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
I have the hundred reasons to not attend the meeting tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I have the hundred reasons.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "hundred" is a cardinal number and when used to indicate an unspecified/general quantity (not a particular, previously mentioned set), it must be preceded by the indefinite article "a", not the definite article "the".

• Rule: We say "a hundred", "a thousand", "a dozen", etc., when referring to a general large quantity — the definite article "the" is used only when a specific, already-identified group of "hundred reasons" is being referred to, which is not the case here.
◦ Example: She gave a hundred excuses for being late (not "the hundred excuses").

• Applying the rule, the phrase "I have the hundred reasons" should correctly read "I have a hundred reasons". This segment therefore contains the grammatical error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "the meeting" is correct as printed — "the" is rightly used here because a specific, particular meeting (already known/referred to) is meant.

• Option 3: "tomorrow" is a correctly used time adverb and needs no article; it is grammatically fine as printed.

• Option 4: "to not attend" is a split infinitive (to + not + attend). While traditional grammar frowns upon splitting an infinitive, modern usage accepts it as grammatically correct, especially in spoken and informal English, so this segment is not considered an error here.

NOTE

• Common exam trap: "the" vs "a/an" before quantity words — always check whether the noun phrase refers to a specific, identified quantity (use "the") or a general/indefinite one (use "a/an").

• Similar errors are frequently tested with "a number of", "a lot of", "a couple of" — remember these idiomatic quantity expressions always take the indefinite article, never "the".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in brackets to fill in the blank.
Sheila ________ (failed) all her classes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. passed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "failed" means to be unsuccessful in an examination, test or attempt. (असफल होना)

• Its antonym is "passed", meaning to succeed in an examination or test by meeting the required standard. (उत्तीर्ण होना/सफल होना)
◦ Example: Sheila passed all her classes with distinction.

• Applying this to the sentence: "Sheila passed all her classes" correctly conveys the opposite meaning of "failed".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "flunked" (फेल होना): This is actually a synonym of "failed" (informal, meaning to fail a test/course), not its antonym — so it is incorrect here.

• Option 3: "fizzled" (धीरे-धीरे समाप्त होना): Means to end weakly or come to nothing after a promising start; it is unrelated to passing/failing an exam.

• Option 4: "flopped" (बुरी तरह असफल होना): Means to fail completely or collapse, again a near-synonym of "failed", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Frequently confused synonym–antonym pairs of "fail/pass" tested in SSC exams: succeed ↔ fail, qualify ↔ disqualify, clear (an exam) ↔ flunk.

• Remember: "flunk", "flop" and "fizzle out" are all informal words associated with failure, not success — a common distractor pattern in antonym questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
All his friends admired him because he was a straight shooter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A thoroughly upright straightforward person.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "straight shooter" means a person who is honest, direct and straightforward in speech and dealings, and does not deceive or mislead others. (एक ईमानदार और स्पष्टवादी व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: Everyone trusted the new manager because she was known to be a straight shooter.

• The expression draws on the image of someone who "shoots straight" — that is, aims and speaks directly without deviation, dishonesty or hidden motives.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Excellent shooter" takes the phrase literally (a person skilled with a gun), which is not the idiomatic meaning intended in the sentence.

• Option 2: "Complicated and confusing person" is the opposite of the intended meaning — a straight shooter is simple and direct, not confusing.

• Option 3: "Miserly and pessimistic individual" is unrelated; the idiom has nothing to do with being stingy or negative.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to honesty/directness frequently asked in SSC exams: "call a spade a spade" (to speak frankly), "in black and white" (in written/clear form), "above board" (open and honest).

• Contrast with idioms of dishonesty: "beat around the bush" (to avoid speaking directly), "play foul" (to act unfairly).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
a large, flat area surrounded by seats used for sports or entertainment
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Arena.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Arena" means a large, flat area surrounded by seats, used for sports events, concerts or other forms of entertainment. (खेल का मैदान/रंगमंच)
◦ Example: The football arena was packed with cheering fans.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Senate" refers to a governing or legislative body/council, not a sports/entertainment venue.

• Option 3: "Department" refers to a division of an organisation, government or institution — unrelated to a seating venue.

• Option 4: "Garden" refers to a piece of ground for growing plants/flowers, not a seated venue for sports or entertainment.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes for venues often asked in SSC exams: "Auditorium" (a hall for public gatherings/performances), "Stadium" (a sports ground with tiered seating), "Amphitheatre" (an oval/circular open-air venue with tiered seating).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
After I retire, I started a second career / as a writer and published several books / which allowed me to share my stories / and insights with a wider audience.
option_1: and insights with a wider audience
option_2: After I retire, I started a second career
option_3: as a writer and published several books
option_4: which allowed me to share my stories
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. After I retire, I started a second career.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The rest of the sentence — "started", "published", "allowed" — is entirely in the Past Tense, describing events that have already happened.

• Rule — Tense Consistency: When a sentence narrates a sequence of past events, all the clauses referring to that timeline must remain in a past tense; an unrelated present-tense verb creates a tense mismatch.

• In the given segment, "After I retire" wrongly uses the Simple Present Tense ("retire"), whereas the timeline of the sentence demands the Simple Past Tense; it should correctly read "After I retired".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "and insights with a wider audience" is grammatically correct — it continues the object of "share" begun in the previous segment.

• Option 3: "as a writer and published several books" is correct — "published" correctly continues the past-tense narration.

• Option 4: "which allowed me to share my stories" is correct — "allowed" is correctly in the past tense, referring back to "published several books".

NOTE

• A common SSC error-spotting trap is mixing present-tense time clauses (after/before/when + present tense) into an otherwise past-tense narrative — always check that subordinate time clauses match the tense of the main narrative when the whole sentence describes a completed past sequence.

• Remember: "after" and "before" can take the present tense only when the main clause is also in the present or future tense (e.g., "After I retire, I will travel").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Celebrate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Rejoice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Celebrate" means to honour a special occasion or achievement with enjoyment and festivity, or to feel great happiness about something. (उत्सव मनाना/खुशी मनाना)

• "Rejoice" means to feel or show great joy or delight, which closely matches the meaning of "celebrate". (आनंदित होना)
◦ Example: The whole team rejoiced when they won the championship.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Daunt" (हतोत्साहित करना): Means to intimidate or discourage someone — the opposite sense of celebrating.

• Option 3: "Bitch" (शिकायत करना - slang): Used informally to mean complaining bitterly; entirely unrelated to celebration.

• Option 4: "Assure" (आश्वासन देना): Means to promise or state confidently to remove doubt — unrelated to festivity or joy.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "celebrate" commonly tested: "revel", "commemorate", "observe" (an occasion).

• "Daunt" is often confused with "taunt" (to mock) — remember "daunt" specifically means to discourage/intimidate.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
The _____________ was decorated with candles and chocolates everywhere.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. floor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a noun naming a surface that can be decorated with candles and chocolates — this is "floor", meaning the flat lower surface of a room.

• Rule — Homophones: Homophones are words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings; the correct one must be chosen based on the meaning required by the context, not by sound alone.

• Here, "floor" fits the context perfectly: "The floor was decorated with candles and chocolates everywhere."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flour" is a homophone of "floor" but means a powder made from grinding grain, used in cooking — it makes no sense in this context.

• Option 2: "flower" refers to the colourful reproductive part of a plant, not a homophone of "floor" and contextually incorrect here.

• Option 4: "flor" is not a standard English word (it is used in Spanish for "flower", and as a specialised term in sherry-making) and does not fit the blank.

NOTE

• Common homophone pairs tested in SSC exams: flour/floor, flower/flour, their/there/they're, its/it's, whether/weather, principal/principle.

• Always decide between homophones using the meaning demanded by the sentence, not the sound of the word.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tangiable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Tangible" — able to be touched or perceived as materially existing; real and definite. (मूर्त/स्पर्श करने योग्य)
◦ Example: The company showed tangible results within the first year.

• Spelling key: TANG + IBLE. The word ends in the suffix "-ible", not "-iable"; the printed option wrongly adds an extra "a" before "ble".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Terracotta" is correctly spelt — a type of brownish-orange fired clay used for pottery and building materials. (टेराकोटा मिट्टी)

• Option 3: "Tertial" is correctly spelt — a term (mainly in ornithology) referring to the innermost flight feathers of a bird's wing.

• Option 4: "Terracide" is correctly spelt as printed in the paper.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ible" vs "-able" are a frequent SSC spelling trap: "-ible" is used with Latin roots that do not form a complete word on their own (tangible, visible, credible, feasible), while "-able" is typically added to complete English words (comfortable, acceptable, reasonable).

• Other commonly confused "-ible" words: possible, responsible, sensible, terrible, horrible.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Occurence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Occurrence" — an incident or event that happens. (घटना)
◦ Example: Earthquakes are a common occurrence in that region.

• Spelling key: OC + CUR + R + ENCE — the letter "r" is doubled after "cur" (occur → occurrence), a doubling that the printed option "Occurence" wrongly omits.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Harassment" is correctly spelt — the act of subjecting someone to persistent, unwanted aggressive pressure.

• Option 3: "Supersede" is correctly spelt — to take the place of, especially due to being more up to date; note it is one of the few English words ending in "-sede" (not "-cede" or "-ceed").

• Option 4: "Exaggerate" is correctly spelt — to represent something as being larger, better, or worse than it really is.

NOTE

• A common SSC spelling rule: when a verb ending in a single stressed vowel + consonant takes a suffix, the final consonant is often doubled (occur → occurred, occurrence; refer → referred; begin → beginning).

• "Supersede" is the ONLY common English word ending in "-sede"; "proceed", "succeed", "exceed" end in "-ceed"; all other similar words end in "-cede" (precede, concede, recede, intercede).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in the brackets to fill in the blank.
She ________ the target by an inch and lost the gold medal. [hit]
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. missed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "hit" here means to successfully strike or reach a target. (निशाना लगाना)

• Its antonym is "missed", meaning to fail to hit or reach the target. (चूक जाना)
◦ Example: The archer missed the bullseye by a fraction of an inch.

• The sentence's own logic confirms this — she "lost the gold medal", which makes sense only if she failed to hit the target, i.e., she missed it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "touched" (छूना): Means to make light contact with something — it does not convey the sense of failing to hit a target.

• Option 2: "bashed" (जोर से मारना): Means to strike violently, which is close in meaning to "hit", not its opposite.

• Option 4: "cleaned" (साफ करना): Means to remove dirt; entirely unrelated to hitting/missing a target.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs related to aim/target frequently tested: hit ↔ miss, strike ↔ dodge, achieve ↔ fail.

• Be careful of near-synonyms like "bashed" and "touched" being used as distractors when the required antonym relates to failure/inaccuracy, not force or contact.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A period of ten years
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Decade.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Decade" means a period of ten years. (दशक)
◦ Example: The city has changed dramatically over the past decade.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Century" refers to a period of one hundred years, not ten.

• Option 3: "Biennium" refers to a period of two years, not ten.

• Option 4: "lustrum" refers to a period of five years, not ten.

NOTE

• Time-period one-word substitutes frequently tested in SSC exams: Lustrum = 5 years, Decade = 10 years, Biennium = 2 years, Century = 100 years, Millennium = 1000 years, Fortnight = 2 weeks.

• Remember the Latin roots: "dec-" relates to ten (decade, decagon), "cent-" relates to hundred (century, centenary), "mille-" relates to thousand (millennium).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
My uncle lives in New York, so I only see him once in a blue moon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Not very often.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "once in a blue moon" means very rarely; hardly ever; not very often. (बहुत कम/कभी-कभार)
◦ Example: He visits his hometown once in a blue moon, as he is settled abroad.

• The phrase alludes to the rare astronomical occurrence of a "blue moon" (a second full moon in the same calendar month), which happens infrequently — hence its association with rarity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Monthly" suggests a fixed regular frequency, which contradicts the idiom's sense of rare, irregular occurrence.

• Option 3: "Weekly" likewise indicates regular frequent occurrence, opposite to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: "Very often" is the direct opposite of the idiom's actual meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms of rarity/frequency tested in SSC exams: "few and far between" (rare), "every now and then" (occasionally), "day in and day out" (very frequently, daily).

• Do not confuse "once in a blue moon" (rare) with "once in a while" (occasionally) — the former indicates far greater rarity.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who eats a lot
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Glutton.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Glutton" means one who eats excessively; a person with a habitually greedy appetite for food. (पेटू व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He is such a glutton that he finishes an entire pizza by himself.

• This one-word substitute exactly matches the given definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Chauffeur" means a person employed to drive a private motor car — unrelated to eating.

• Option 2: "Steward" means a person who manages another's property, or an attendant on a ship/aircraft — unrelated to eating a lot.

• Option 4: "Chef" means a professional cook, especially the chief cook in a restaurant — a chef prepares food but is not defined by eating a lot.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes on food/eating habits: "Gourmet" (a connoisseur of good food), "Epicure" (one devoted to sensual/food pleasures), "Herbivore" (an animal that eats only plants), "Omnivore" (one that eats both plants and meat).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
I was happy to know that Sheila passed her final exams.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Sad.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "happy" means feeling or showing pleasure or contentment. (खुश)

• Its antonym is "sad", meaning feeling or showing sorrow; unhappy. (दुखी)
◦ Example: She was sad to hear that the trip had been cancelled.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Joyful" (आनंदित): Is a synonym of "happy", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "upbeat" (उत्साहित): Means cheerful and optimistic — again a synonym of "happy", not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Excited" (उत्साहित/उत्तेजित): Means feeling great enthusiasm; it is close in spirit to "happy" rather than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs of "happy" tested in SSC exams: happy ↔ miserable, happy ↔ gloomy, cheerful ↔ dejected.

• Watch out for options that are actually synonyms (joyful, upbeat, excited) being placed as distractors in antonym questions — always double check the direction of meaning asked.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym for the underlined word in the given sentence.
One of Ram's leisure activities is tennis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Recreation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "leisure" means free time spent away from work or duties, used for relaxation or enjoyment. (फुर्सत/मनोरंजन)

• "Recreation" means an activity done for enjoyment when one is not working, which closely matches the meaning of "leisure" in this context. (मनोरंजन)
◦ Example: Reading is one of my favourite recreation activities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Main" (मुख्य): Means primary or most important — unrelated to leisure/free time.

• Option 2: "Lead" (नेतृत्व करना/प्रमुख): Means to guide or the principal role — unrelated to the concept of leisure.

• Option 3: "Languish" (कमजोर पड़ना/तड़पना): Means to lose vitality or suffer neglect — the opposite mood of enjoyable leisure.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "leisure" often tested: "relaxation", "free time", "pastime".

• Do not confuse "leisure" (free time) with "leisurely" (unhurried, relaxed in manner, e.g. "a leisurely walk").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word segment in the given sentence.
The wedding was put on until January.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. put off.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a phrasal verb meaning to postpone or delay an event to a later time.

• "Put off" means precisely to postpone; to delay something until a later time.
◦ Example: The meeting was put off until next week due to the manager's absence.

• Applying this: "The wedding was put off until January" correctly conveys that the wedding was postponed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "put in" means to submit/install/insert something (e.g., put in an application) — it does not mean to postpone.

• Option 3: "put down" means to write something down, to suppress, or to belittle someone — unrelated to postponing.

• Option 4: "put up" means to erect/build something, or to provide accommodation — unrelated to postponing.

NOTE

• Phrasal verbs with "put" are frequently tested in SSC exams: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), put across (communicate clearly), put forward (propose), put away (store/save).

• Do not confuse "put off" (postpone) with "call off" (cancel entirely) — postponing means rescheduling to a later date, while cancelling means the event will not happen at all.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The children have made the box.
option_1: The box is being made by the children.
option_3: The box had been made by the children.
option_4: The box has been made by the children.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The box has been made by the children.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The children have made the box" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + have/has + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the box" becomes the subject; since "box" is singular, the auxiliary is "has"; the verb "made" (already V3) is retained; and "the children" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The box has been made by the children.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "is being made" is the passive form of the Present Continuous Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it is not a passive sentence at all — "Children had made the box" is an active sentence in the Past Perfect Tense, and it also drops the article "The" before "children".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been made" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• The Present Perfect passive structure "has/have been + V3" is one of the most frequently tested tense-passive combinations in SSC exams — do not confuse it with the Past Perfect passive "had been + V3".

• Remember: choice of "has" vs "have" in the passive depends on the number/person of the new subject (the original object), exactly as in the active voice.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. The upper part of the river
B. Continuous rain on
C. Week, there had been
D. During the previous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. DCBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A meaningful sentence must begin with a time-setting phrase, followed by the main clause (subject + verb), and end with the object/complement that the verb acts upon.

• Part D ("During the previous") naturally begins the sentence, as it sets the time frame, and logically connects with C ("week, there had been") to complete the phrase "During the previous week, there had been...".

• This is followed by B ("Continuous rain on"), which supplies the subject "continuous rain" of the existential clause, and finally A ("the upper part of the river"), which completes the sentence by specifying where the rain fell.

• Combining in the order D-C-B-A: "During the previous week, there had been continuous rain on the upper part of the river." — this reads as a complete, grammatically correct and meaningful sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "DBAC" breaks the sentence into "During the previous continuous rain on the upper part of the river week, there had been", which is grammatically incoherent.

• Option 3: "ADCB" produces "The upper part of the river during the previous week, there had been continuous rain on", which is disjointed and unnatural.

• Option 4: "ABCD" produces "The upper part of the river continuous rain on week, there had been during the previous", which is meaningless.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-jumble questions, first identify the part that logically must open the sentence (often a time/place phrase or a proper noun/subject), then locate the part containing the main verb, and build outward — checking that each transition reads naturally.

• Existential "there had been/there was" constructions in Past Perfect Tense are commonly tested in SSC para-jumbles.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
They are organising a concert for charity.
option_1: A concert is being organised by them for charity.
option_2: They are organising a charity concert.
option_3: They are being organised a concert for charity.
option_4: A concert for charity is organising by them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A concert is being organised by them for charity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "They are organising a concert for charity" is in the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a concert" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary is "is"; the verb "organising" becomes "being organised"; and "they" becomes the agent with "by", while the adverbial phrase "for charity" is retained at the end.
◦ Passive: A concert is being organised by them for charity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "They are organising a charity concert" is an active sentence, not a passive one; it does not answer the question.

• Option 3: "They are being organised a concert for charity" is incorrect because "they" (the doer) cannot be made the grammatical subject of a passive sentence in this way — the verb "organise" cannot take "they" as its passive subject when "a concert" is the true object.

• Option 4: "A concert for charity is organising by them" is incorrect because the passive auxiliary "being" has been omitted; it should be "is being organised", not "is organising".

NOTE

• A common distractor in passive-voice questions is a sentence that drops the auxiliary "being" from the continuous passive — always check that "being" is present before the past participle in continuous-tense passives.

• Remember the fixed passive pattern for continuous tenses: is/am/are/was/were + being + V3.

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct logical sequence.
A. When we connect this design with a wire, electricity flows.
B. These metal strips were put in a sulphuric acid solution.
C. He made two strips of different metals.
D. Alessandro Volta discovered electric battery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. DCBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A logically sequenced passage must move from the general introduction of the topic/subject to specific supporting details, in chronological order of events.

• Sentence D ("Alessandro Volta discovered electric battery") must open the passage, as it introduces the subject (Volta) and the topic (the electric battery) before any pronoun referring to him ("He") is used.

• This is naturally followed by C ("He made two strips of different metals"), where "He" refers back to Volta, describing his first step in building the battery.

• Next comes B ("These metal strips were put in a sulphuric acid solution"), where "These metal strips" refers back to the strips mentioned in C, describing the next step.

• Finally, A ("When we connect this design with a wire, electricity flows") concludes the passage, describing the outcome once the whole apparatus ("this design") is complete.

• Combining in the order D-C-B-A gives a coherent, chronological account of how Volta invented the electric battery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "CBDA" begins with "He made two strips..." without first identifying who "He" is, which is incoherent as an opening.

• Option 3: "BCDA" begins by referring to "these metal strips" before any strips have been introduced, making the pronoun reference unclear.

• Option 4: "ACDB" begins with the result ("electricity flows") before the apparatus or the strips have even been described, reversing the logical/causal order.

NOTE

• In jumbled-sentence questions, look for the sentence that introduces the proper noun/subject (here, "Alessandro Volta") before it is replaced by a pronoun ("He") — this sentence almost always opens the sequence.

• Also track referential words like "these", "this", "he", "it" — they must always follow the sentence that first introduces the noun they refer back to.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Earthquake is the (1)__________ breaking and displacement of substantial portions of the earth's outer rocky crust. During an earthquake, rock disturbances can cause rivers to change their flow. Landslides (2)__________ by earthquakes can cause significant destruction and loss of life. Tsunamis are a (3)__________ of damaging waves caused by large earthquakes that occur under the ocean. Earthquakes rarely directly kill anyone. Many (4)__________ and injuries are caused by falling debris and the fall of structures. The (5)__________ of an earthquake relies on how much and how far rock cracks and shifts.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. abrupt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the nature of the "breaking and displacement of substantial portions of the earth's outer rocky crust" that defines an earthquake — this breaking is sudden and without warning.

• "Abrupt" means sudden and unexpected, which correctly describes the nature of the crustal breaking that causes an earthquake.

• Applying this: "Earthquake is the abrupt breaking and displacement..." correctly conveys that earthquakes occur suddenly, without gradual warning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "innovative" means new and original in method/idea — it does not describe a physical, sudden geological breaking.

• Option 2: "expansive" means covering a wide area, or (of a person) open and talkative — it does not capture the suddenness that defines an earthquake.

• Option 3: "deliberate" means done consciously and intentionally — earthquakes are natural events, not intentional acts, so this word is contextually wrong.

NOTE

• In cloze passages about natural disasters, look for words describing suddenness/intensity: "abrupt", "sudden", "violent", "unexpected" are common correct fits for describing seismic events.

• Do not be misled by words that sound scientific/formal (like "expansive" or "deliberate") if they do not match the precise sense demanded by the sentence.

Landslides (2)__________ by earthquakes can cause significant destruction and loss of life. Tsunamis are a (3)__________ of damaging waves caused by large earthquakes that occur under the ocean. Earthquakes rarely directly kill anyone. Many (4)__________ and injuries are caused by falling debris and the fall of structures. The (5)__________ of an earthquake relies on how much and how far rock cracks and shifts.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. triggered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes how landslides are set off/caused by earthquakes.

• "Triggered" means caused to happen suddenly, or set off, which is exactly the relationship between an earthquake and a landslide it causes.

• Applying this: "Landslides triggered by earthquakes can cause significant destruction and loss of life" correctly conveys that earthquakes are the cause that sets off landslides.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "subdued" means brought under control or made quieter — the opposite of causing something to happen.

• Option 3: "blocked" means obstructed or stopped — this would mean the earthquake prevents landslides, which contradicts the passage's point that earthquakes cause destruction through landslides.

• Option 4: "prevented" means stopped from happening — again the opposite of the intended cause-and-effect relationship.

NOTE

• Cloze passages describing cause-and-effect relationships between natural events often test words like "triggered", "caused", "induced", "set off" versus their opposites ("prevented", "blocked", "averted") — read the surrounding sentence carefully to determine whether a cause or a prevention is being described.

• "Trigger" is frequently used in scientific/news writing for one natural event causing another (e.g., "the storm triggered flooding").

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. succession.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes what a tsunami consists of — "a ___ of damaging waves" — meaning a tsunami is not a single wave but a series of waves arriving one after another.

• "Succession" means a number of things following one after another in order, which correctly describes a tsunami as a series/sequence of large waves.

• Applying this: "Tsunamis are a succession of damaging waves caused by large earthquakes" correctly describes tsunamis as consisting of multiple consecutive waves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "interruption" means a break or disruption in continuity — it does not describe a set of waves.

• Option 2: "arrest" means the act of stopping something, or a legal detention — neither sense fits "a ___ of damaging waves".

• Option 3: "disorder" means a state of confusion or lack of order — it does not convey the sense of a sequential series of waves.

NOTE

• Scientifically, a tsunami is indeed defined as a series/succession of ocean waves, not a single wave — this real-world fact helps confirm the correct word in this cloze.

• Related words meaning "a series of things one after another": "sequence", "series", "chain", "progression".

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by "and injuries are caused by falling debris and the fall of structures" — the passage is discussing deaths and injuries caused indirectly by earthquakes.

• "Fatalities" means deaths resulting from an accident or disaster, which pairs naturally with "injuries" in describing the human toll of falling debris and collapsing structures.

• Applying this: "Many fatalities and injuries are caused by falling debris and the fall of structures" correctly conveys that earthquakes indirectly cause deaths and injuries.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "survival" means the state of continuing to live — it is the opposite of what pairs meaningfully with "injuries" in a sentence about harm caused by falling debris.

• Option 3: "durability" means the ability to withstand wear and last long — it describes objects/materials, not human casualties, so it does not fit "Many ___ and injuries".

• Option 4: "viability" means the ability to work successfully or survive/function — again this does not fit the context of deaths and injuries.

NOTE

• The passage's earlier sentence — "Earthquakes rarely directly kill anyone" — is a strong contextual clue: the next sentence must explain how deaths (fatalities) do occur, i.e., indirectly through falling debris and structural collapse.

• Common word pairing in disaster-related writing: "fatalities and injuries", "casualties and damage" — remembering such collocations helps in cloze passages.

Landslides (2)__________ by earthquakes can cause significant destruction and loss of life. Tsunamis are a (3)__________ of damaging waves caused by large earthquakes that occur under the ocean. Earthquakes rarely directly kill anyone. Many (4)__________ and injuries are caused by falling debris and the fall of structures. The (5)__________ of an earthquake relies on how much and how far rock cracks and shifts.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. magnitude.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by "of an earthquake relies on how much and how far rock cracks and shifts" — this describes the measured strength/size of an earthquake.

• "Magnitude" means the size, extent or strength of something, especially as used to measure the power of an earthquake, which correctly fits this scientific description.

• Applying this: "The magnitude of an earthquake relies on how much and how far rock cracks and shifts" correctly conveys that an earthquake's strength depends on the extent of rock movement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "depth" refers to how far down something is, which is a different, specific parameter (focal depth) and not the general term for an earthquake's overall strength as described here.

• Option 2: "corpse" means a dead body — entirely irrelevant to the physical description of an earthquake's strength.

• Option 3: "discipline" means a branch of knowledge, or controlled behaviour — unrelated to the measurement of an earthquake's power.

NOTE

• In real-world usage, earthquake strength is measured on the "Richter magnitude scale" or "moment magnitude scale" — reinforcing "magnitude" as the standard scientific term for earthquake size.

• Do not confuse "magnitude" (overall size/strength) with "intensity" (the effect felt at a particular location) — both are real seismology terms but measure different things.
